# df-elect — spec

## Maturity

**Grade:** 4 · S4 E3 A2 H1 P3 · limited by scope (mvp) *(generated by `zig build gen-catalog`)*

**Scope:** mvp — FRRouting/frr EVPN DF election, RFC 7432 §8.5, RFC 8584 (surveyed 2026-09-30; poc -> mvp 2026-09-30: N members, mod N / HRW / preference, failover)
**Audit:** review 2026-10-01 · mutation 2026-10-01 (33/37, 4 eq) · src ?

**Hardening:** fuzz 2026-10-01 (sweep 120 seeds Debug/400 opt (sim)) · ct n/a — multicast DF election (keyword review, 2026-10-07)

**Performance:** not measured

**Known defects:** none recorded

**Downstream consumer:** no

Designated-Forwarder election with failover + split-horizon for N-member
segments of a link-state L2VPN fabric, verified in `netsim` and compared with
FRRouting run as a black box. Usage: see ./README.md. Provenance (clean-room
from RFC 7432 / RFC 8584; FRR observed, never read): see ./README.md; no
third-party terms to restate in /NOTICE.

## Compared with

Surveyed 2026-09-30 per `SURVEY-PLAYBOOK.md`; stars and activity as of that date. No foreign source was read; FRR's licence is quoted from its README ("GPLv2+"), so its source is off limits. There is no library-shaped DF election in Rust, Go or Zig to compare with; the competition is EVPN inside BGP daemons.

| Project | Language | Licence | Stars | Last release / push | What a user notices against this module |

Fails over in ~0.1–0.2 s when the DF's ES link goes down or the DF container is stopped (route withdrawal / session loss in a lab with short BGP timers). Always preempts (no don't-preempt knob): a returning higher-preference PE takes the role back within ~0.3 s, with no visible DF wait. Transients seen: a brief dual DF when one PE's preference was raised, and a 20–30 s dual DF after a PE restart — the restarted PE declared itself DF ~3.6 s after start with no BGP peers, and the stand-in DF kept the role until BGP re-established. Two passes, identical DF outcomes, timings within ~100 ms. |

**Where we are ahead:** the only reusable, dependency-free DF decision for a fabric without BGP; all three DF algorithms in the RFC 8584 registry that matter (mod N, HRW, preference) behind one function; the failover guarantees are stated as bounds and model-checked under partitions, one-way cuts, crashes, restarts and clock jumps — a restarted member starts blocked and cannot produce the long post-restart dual DF observed in FRR. **Where we are behind:** no BGP (by design — the input is a Hello flood), so a failover waits for Hello staleness plus `df_wait` instead of a route withdrawal; the preference algorithm has no "don't preempt" option and no per-tag preference ranges; no RFC 8584 §4 AC-influenced DF; liveness is an abstract `stale_after` threshold, not a real LSA machinery (→ Backlog).

## The problem

A customer site multihomed to N edge nodes (an *edge segment*; an EVPN
Ethernet Segment) needs, for every Ethernet tag on it, exactly one member to
deliver multi-destination (BUM) traffic toward the site — the Designated
Forwarder (DF) — or the site receives every broadcast twice, or not at all.
EVPN gets the membership list "for free" from BGP: each PE advertises an
Ethernet Segment route, BGP's session liveness and withdrawal decide who is
on the list, and the DF is a function of that list (RFC 7432 §8.5 service
carving, or RFC 8584 §3.2 HRW). A link-state fabric has no BGP session to
lean on. It floods Hellos, and each member must derive its roles from what
that flood tells it. That derivation, and what it can and cannot guarantee,
is this module.

Three failure modes, three different guarantees:

- **Split-horizon reflection** — a frame delivered back into the segment it
  came from — is a live loop into the customer's site. **Zero tolerance.**
- **Duplicate delivery** — two members delivering one frame. With failover it
  cannot be zero (below). **Bounded**: only right after connectivity returns.
- **Zero DF** — nobody delivers a tag. **Bounded**: a dead DF is replaced
  within `maxZeroDfWindow` of the last disruption.

## Design & invariants

### The DF function (`election.zig`)

`designatedForwarder(algorithm, esi, candidates, tag)` names the DF among the
candidates — the members a node currently counts as alive, itself included,
in `EdgeSegment.members` order (sorted by address, which `validate` enforces):

- `.modulo` — RFC 7432 §8.5 step 3: the member at ordinal `tag mod N`.
- `.hrw` — RFC 8584 §3.2: the member with the highest
  `Wrand(V, Es, Si) = (1103515245((1103515245·Si + 12345) XOR D(V, Es)) + 12345) mod 2^31`,
  `D` = CRC-32 of the 4-octet tag followed by the 10-octet ESI (network order),
  MSB dropped; ties to the numerically least address. Computed in wrapping
  `u32` and masked, exact because every operation commutes with reduction
  mod 2^31. Removing a member that is not the DF never moves a role (the
  property RFC 8584 argues for HRW over mod N).
- `.preference` — the member with the highest `Member.pref` (default 32767)
  is DF for every tag of the segment, ties to the numerically least address:
  DF algorithm type 2 in the RFC 8584 registry, and what FRRouting's EVPN
  multihoming runs. The rule was taken from FRR's observed behaviour (twelve
  settled phases, `frr_test.zig`); the preference-based draft was not read,
  so its "don't preempt" option and per-tag preference ranges are absent.

Pure: two members with the same candidate list name the same DF, so no vote
is needed. `kat_test.zig` checks both functions against an independent Python
re-derivation (`tools/rederive.py`, CRC-32 from `zlib`, unbounded integers).

### The role state machine (`election.stepRole`)

Per `<segment, tag>` each member holds a `Role`. When its view stops naming
it, it gives the role up **at once**; when its view names it, it takes the
role only after the view has done so **continuously for `df_wait`** (RFC 7432
§8.5 step 2's timer, RFC 8584 §2.1's DF_Wait). `DfElect.init` refuses
`df_wait <= hello_period`: the wait has to cover the first Hello round, or
startup races (below).

### What a member counts as alive, and the view consensus (`protocol.zig`)

Every fabric node floods Hellos, members and non-members alike (a
non-member's Hello carries `types.no_segment`), as every router of a
link-state fabric floods its LSPs. A member counts a peer as alive while the
peer's last Hello is no older than `stale_after`, measured on the member's OWN
clock (netsim's per-node clock, which the fuzzer jumps), and that Hello does
not declare the peer isolated (below). Every Hello carries the sender's view —
a bitmask of the members it currently sees, itself included. A member is
**named** for a tag only when:

1. the DF function over its own view names it, AND
2. the DF function over the last advertised view of **every peer it sees**
   names it too.

Condition 2 exists because the fuzzer found the case without it: netsim's
`link_down` is directional, and a member whose outbound link died keeps
hearing its peers while they stop hearing it. They carve its tags among
themselves; it still names itself; both deliver, with no heal in sight. With
the consensus, the peers' advertised views (which no longer contain it) make
it yield. EVPN gets the same effect from BGP sessions being two-way. The cost
is at most one extra Hello period before a gain (a peer's view is up to one
period old), which the zero-DF bound absorbs.

**Core isolation.** The consensus alone has the mirror-image hole, found by
review 2026-10-01: a member whose INBOUND path died hears nothing, so its view
holds only itself and it names itself DF for every tag — while its peers,
which still hear it, defer to that view. It held every role and received no
frame: the segment got no traffic at all, for as long as the cut lasted, and
the zero-DF check (which counts holders) saw nothing wrong. Now a member that
has heard no fabric node for `stale_after` (or not yet since it started) is
**isolated**: its view is empty — without even its own bit — so it is named
for nothing, and the Hellos it still manages to send tell its peers to stop
counting it. This is EVPN-MH "core isolation" as FRRouting applies it (access
ports go protodown once every uplink is gone). It is also why non-members
flood Hellos: a lone surviving member must hear the fabric even when all its
peers are dead.

**Known limit.** A one-way failure deeper in the core — core1 no longer hears
core0 and core2 while they still hear it — leaves the member behind core1
hearing core1 (so not isolated) but no peer: it claims every tag and receives
nothing, and its peers defer to its single-member view. From the members'
side this looks exactly like the outbound case above, where deferring is
right; telling them apart needs the directed fabric graph, which a flood of
segment views does not carry (Backlog). `known limit: …` in `protocol.zig`
pins it. The fuzz sweep never drew this schedule in 1 200 runs (it needs two
specific unrepaired one-way core cuts at once).

A restarted member starts with no role and an empty view (RFC 7432 §8.5: a PE
starts blocked); its Hellos and timers carry a start epoch so a timer armed
before a crash cannot double the new chain.

### Why duplicates are bounded, not zero

Until 2026-09-30 this module elected a static owner per segment and never
failed over: `is_df` ignored liveness, which bought zero duplicates and cost
availability without bound (a dead owner black-holed the segment for good).
The argument behind it still holds and is exactly what failover costs: a
member decides from its local view, and a Hello flood cannot distinguish
"peer dead" from "peer cut off from me". During a real partition each side
legitimately carves the tags among its own members (no frame reaches both
sides, so no duplicate). When the partition heals, a BUM frame and the next
Hello race across the healed cut; until the Hello lands, both sides' DFs for
a tag still hold the role, and a frame that reaches both is delivered twice.
Giving up at once keeps that window to the time a Hello needs to arrive;
nothing local can close it. EVPN accepts the same window (RFC 8584 §1.3).

Startup is different and is duplicate-free: every member's first view holds
only itself, so every view names itself DF for every tag, and without the
wait each would deliver at once. `df_wait > hello_period` + flood delay lets
the first Hellos shrink those claims before any role is taken. The negative
control runs `df_wait = 0` and duplicates at startup with no fault to explain
it.

### Split-horizon (`election.allowForward`)

A frame may be delivered to a segment unless it ingressed from that segment.
Independent of DF state and liveness by design: it is RFC 7432 §8.3's
local-bias backstop and must hold inside a dual-DF window too.
`types.no_ingress` differs from every real segment id by construction.

### How each invariant is checked (`checks.zig`)

1. **Split-horizon, live**: `DeliveryChecker` sets a sticky violation that
   netsim's `checkFn` raises on the same event, capturing the reproducer.
2. **Duplicates, post-run**: every second delivery of a frame to a segment is
   recorded with its time; `firstUnexplainedDuplicate` requires each one to
   follow a heal, link-up or node restart within `maxDuplicateWindow` =
   `2·hello_period` (the next Hello, plus a period of flood budget). The
   positive control and the fault-free runs set `duplicates_fatal`.
3. **Zero-DF, post-run**: `worstZeroDfWindow` rebuilds, per `<segment, tag>`,
   which SERVING members hold the role — serving = up and reachable from
   some other live node over the links the fault trace leaves up (a member
   nothing reaches receives no frame, so neither its holding a role nor its
   lacking one means anything) — and measures every stretch with no serving
   holder while a member was serving, from startup or the LAST disruptive
   fault before it ended (link/partition/crash/restart/clock-jump;
   single-message faults are not disruptions — one lost Hello never flips
   liveness). The bound `maxZeroDfWindow` = `stale_after + df_wait +
   3·hello_period` (= 470): detection plus the tick that notices it, the
   peers re-advertising their views, the wait, and the evaluation tick (the
   isolation path is the slow one; flood delays fit the slack because
   evaluation also runs on every BUM frame). A schedule that keeps disrupting
   can keep a tag without a DF — true of any failover protocol — so the bound
   is a recovery bound. Two DFs at once is not measured as bad: across a
   partition it is the design, and where it matters (one frame reaching both)
   it shows up in (2).
4. **Lost frames, post-run**: `firstUnexplainedLoss` takes every frame put
   on the fabric and requires each segment that carries its tag (other than
   its ingress) to have received it, unless the frame left within
   `maxZeroDfWindow` of startup or of a disruption or `drop_once`, a fault
   came while it was in flight (`maxDuplicateWindow`), or no live member was
   reachable from its origin. This is the check that sees what (3) cannot
   by construction — traffic, not role bookkeeping — and it is what caught
   the isolation hole in the sweep (seed 66) once it existed.

## Threat model / out of scope

Not a security boundary; the adversary is timing and topology (netsim's fault
fuzzer: partitions and heals, one-way link cuts and repairs, crashes and
restarts, clock jumps, single-message drop/dup/delay). The flood's CONTENT is
trusted — a lying Hello (a forged view) is out of scope, as is node
authentication. Out of scope too: RFC 8584 §4 AC-influenced DF, the
preference algorithm's "don't preempt" option and per-tag ranges (see
Backlog), VLAN bundles beyond using the lowest VLAN as the tag, and
multi-segment split-horizon label interactions.

**Malformed frames are NOT trusted, though.** `tagOf` / `Hello.decode` /
`BumFrame.decode` return `DecodeError!T` (`Truncated` / `InvalidEncoding`) and
bounds-check before indexing; both messages are 17 octets and the tag byte is
what separates them, so each decoder checks it. `origin` and `seq` are
untrusted values too: `origin` indexes `node_count*node_count` arrays and
`seq` is a shift into a u64 bitmask, so both are range-checked in the
handlers against the live topology; a Hello's `view` bits past the member
list are masked off. Policy: drop and count (`DfElect.malformed_dropped`,
asserted 0 across the sweep, since every frame in the harness is our own).

**Harness simplifications.** BUM traffic is timer-generated (`bum_period`),
bounded to < 64 originations per origin so the per-origin dedup is a 64-bit
bitmask; a real data plane would use a windowed set. Evaluation runs on the
Hello tick and on every received Hello/BUM frame, not on a dedicated DF-wait
timer, which is why the bounds carry one Hello period of granularity.
Delivery to "the segment" is abstract: a member that receives a frame and
holds the role for its tag delivers it; there is no CE-side link to fail
separately from the member (an access-link failure is modelled as the member
leaving, which RFC 7432 also does by withdrawing its ES route).

## Verification

`zig build test-df-elect` (54 tests):

- **Fuzz sweep**, all three algorithms, 120 seeds in Debug and 400 optimized, every
  fault kind enabled: zero split-horizon violations; every duplicate explained
  by a heal/link-up/restart within 100 ticks (measured worst 44 both modes,
  2026-10-01); worst zero-DF 363 Debug / 409 optimized against the 470
  bound; no unexplained lost frame; no frame of our own ever dropped as
  malformed; the heal race really happens (duplicates > 0 asserted). The
  measurements live in a comment, not on stderr (the lanes fail a passing
  step that writes there); a failure prints the fault schedule and the
  `<segment, tag>`'s DF transitions.
- **One-way member cuts**: inbound (`core1→4`, `core2→7`: the member goes
  deaf, gives every role up, the segment keeps receiving) and outbound
  (`4→core1`, `7→core2`: it yields to the peers' carving, no duplicate) —
  the first failed before core isolation, 16 of 16 frames lost. The deeper
  core asymmetry is pinned as a known limit.
- **Fault-free**: no duplicate at all (`duplicates_fatal`), the roles settle on
  the RFC assignment over all members (`settledDf`), the startup zero window
  is real (> 0, the wait is observed) and within the bound.
- **Failover**: the DF of a tag crashes at t=400 — a survivor holds it before
  the restart, the zero window stays within bound, no duplicate (a restarted
  member starts blocked), and after the restart the RFC assignment returns.
- **Partition/heal**: the isolated member carves every tag for itself during
  the cut, every duplicate is explained by the heal, and the roles settle.
- **Negative control**: `df_wait = 0` duplicates at startup, unexplained; the
  config check refuses it.
- **Positive control**: `BrokenAlwaysDf` trips the checker on one seed, across
  a 100-seed sweep, and shrinks to the empty fault set.
- **EXTERNAL** (`frr_test.zig`): the preference choice in 12 settled phases
  observed from FRRouting 10.7.1, and a control that mod N and HRW do not
  reproduce them.
- **REDERIVED** (`kat_test.zig`): 4 cases, 20 tags, 64 HRW weights and both DF
  functions against `tools/rederive.py`.
- **Mutation run 2026-10-01** (schemata, ReleaseSafe, 37 mutants over the
  DF functions, `stepRole`, the protocol's liveness/isolation/consensus/
  input guards and every analyzer): 33 killed. The first pass left 8; four
  missing tests were added (the timer start-epoch guard, view bits past the
  member list, a member's Hello naming another segment or none, the
  `df_wait == hello_period` edge). Four are equivalent: the HRW digest's
  MSB mask (multiplication mod 2^31 drops bit 31), `>` vs `>=` at exactly
  `stale_after`, not clearing `last_heard` on restart (with `df_wait +
  hello_period > stale_after` a restarted member is isolated before it could
  gain), and evaluating roles on BUM arrival (only granularity; the bounds
  hold without it).
- **Units**: the DF functions (even load for mod N, HRW minimal disruption and
  tie-break), `stepRole` (immediate loss, continuous-wait gain, interrupted
  wait), `allowForward`, `EdgeSegment.validate`, the codecs (round trips,
  fail-closed decoding, fuzz corpora), the checker and both post-run analyzers
  against synthetic logs (startup, crashed holder, all members down, window
  measured from the last disruption, two holders not counted, an unreachable
  member neither serving nor holding), and `firstUnexplainedLoss` (each
  explanation, its edges, and what is not owed at all).

## Backlog / deferred

- **Directed fabric graph.** Let every Hello carry the set of nodes its sender
  hears (an adjacency LSP); each member can then compute which members the
  BUM sources reach and carve among those, replacing the deference heuristic
  and closing the known limit (a one-way failure deeper in the core).
- ~~Segments with more than two members~~ — done 2026-09-30 (N members, per-tag DF).
- ~~RFC 8584 HRW~~, ~~preference-based DF~~ — done 2026-09-30. Left of the
  preference algorithm: the "don't preempt" option (a returning
  higher-preference member does not take the role back) and per-tag
  preference ranges. Fits §2.
- A real LSA age/refresh liveness model in place of the abstract `stale_after`
  threshold, if this graduates from a model-checked jewel into a fabric
  component (`isis-sim` now has one to borrow).
- A dedicated DF-wait timer instead of evaluating on the Hello tick, which
  would take one `hello_period` of granularity out of both bounds.
- RFC 8584 §4 AC-influenced DF (a member whose attachment circuit for a tag is
  down drops out of that tag's candidate list).

## Status

`any · util · single_owner` + dep `netsim` — canonical source is `pub const
meta` in src/root.zig.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class B · oracle MIXED

- **Class B** — published cryptographic or algorithmic construction with published vectors.
- **Oracle MIXED** — anchored for some paths, self for others — the evidence below names which.

**What the tests actually contain.** EXTERNAL: `src/frr_test.zig` — the preference-based DF choice in 12 settled phases observed from FRRouting 10.7.1 run as a black box (`tools/frr/`, raw observations committed under `tools/frr/observed/`): equal and distinct preferences, preference raised, lowered and reset to the default, the DF's ES link down and back, the DF PE down and back; a control shows mod N and HRW do not reproduce those choices. REDERIVED: `src/kat_test.zig` — mod N (RFC 7432 §8.5) and HRW (RFC 8584 §3.2) against an independent Python re-derivation (`tools/rederive.py`: `zlib` CRC-32, unbounded integers), 20 tags and 64 weights. SELF: the protocol — failover, the view consensus, the duplicate and zero-DF bounds — is model-checked in `netsim` against invariants stated here, with positive and negative controls, not against a foreign implementation; FRR's timings are recorded in "Compared with" but not asserted (different liveness source, different time base).

**How it got there.** Until 2026-09-30 the module was class D (its own static two-member election, oracle n/a). Moving to the RFC algorithms made an outside truth exist, so the class is B; the FRR lab gave the preference algorithm an external oracle and the RFC formulas a re-derivation.
